# Macronutrients: carbohydrate, fat, protein and fibre

> *Carbohydrate, fat and protein supply the body's energy, and two plates with the same energy content
> can have very different effects on health. We take each nutrient in turn, including the glycaemic
> index, fibre and the shape of fatty acids, and then show how the nutrients combine into dietary
> patterns.*

::: {.callout-note}
## Learning objectives
- Explain how the length and branching of carbohydrate chains set how fast a food raises blood glucose.
- Distinguish glycaemic index from glycaemic load, and explain why portion size can change the verdict
  on a high-GI food.
- Explain how saturation and *cis*/*trans* geometry shape a fatty acid, and rank dietary fats by
  cardiovascular risk.
- Describe how amino-acid sequence sets protein structure and function, and how complementary plant
  proteins cover each other's gaps.
- Outline how carbohydrate, fat and protein are digested and absorbed, and where each enters the
  circulation.
- State the fibre and wholegrain evidence with its caveat, and give quality-based advice based on
  My Healthy Plate, referring restrictive diets to a dietitian.
:::

::: {.concept-tree}
[Chapter map]{.tree-title}

- [Carbohydrate](#sec-carbohydrate): from free sugars to wholegrains
  - [Glycaemic index and glycaemic load](#sec-gi-gl): the speed and size of the glucose rise
  - [Fibre](#sec-fibre): the carbohydrate we don't digest
- [Fat](#sec-dietary-fat): type matters more than total
- [Protein](#sec-protein): from amino acids to quality
- [From nutrients to patterns](#sec-nutrient-patterns): foods and patterns, not ratios
:::

## Macronutrients at a glance {#sec-overview}

**Macronutrients** are the nutrients the body needs in gram quantities, and the ones that supply
energy. There are three (carbohydrate, fat and protein), plus **dietary fibre**, the carbohydrate
that the small intestine cannot digest. They differ in how much energy each yields:

| Macronutrient | Energy (kcal/g) | Main role |
|---|---|---|
| Carbohydrate | ~4 | Primary, glucose-yielding fuel |
| Fat | ~9 | Energy store, cell membranes, essential fatty acids |
| Protein | ~4 | Structure, enzymes, immune & transport functions |
| Fibre | ~2 | Fermented by gut microbes; not a fuel in the usual sense |
| *(Alcohol)* | *~7* | *Not a nutrient; empty calories, shown for contrast* |

Fat is the most energy-dense macronutrient, so fat-rich foods raise total intake quickly.

::: {.callout-important}
## What decides a macronutrient's health effect
The health effect of a macronutrient depends on its form and food source, so "Are carbs bad?" and
"Is fat bad?" have no single answer. The question that matters clinically is almost never "how many
grams?" but "what kind, from what food?" (see [Are carbs bad?](#sec-close)).
:::

## Carbohydrate {#sec-carbohydrate}

**What it is.** Carbohydrates run a wide spectrum, and where a food sits on it matters far
more than the word "carb":

::: {.spectrum}
[The carbohydrate spectrum]{.tree-title}

- Free sugars and refined starches
- Intact wholegrains and fibre

[Limit]{.spectrum-end} [Protective]{.spectrum-end}
:::

Each region of the spectrum has its own place in the diet:

- **Free sugars**, added sugars plus those in honey, syrups and fruit juices, are the carbohydrate to
  limit. The WHO caps them at <10% of energy, with further benefit below 5% [@who2020diet]. The
  natural sugar inside whole fruit is not a free sugar and is not the target.
- **Refined starches** (white rice, white bread) are digested fast and stripped of fibre.
- **Wholegrains**, grains that keep their bran and germ, sit with fibre at the protective end.

![Whatever their source, digestible carbohydrates are broken down to simple sugars, chiefly glucose, shown here in its ring form.](/figures/structures/beta-d-glucose.svg){#fig-glucose fig-alt="Skeletal ring structure of beta-D-glucose." width="230"}

Every digestible carbohydrate is built from simple sugars, and the length and shape of the chain
decide how fast it becomes blood glucose. Four terms describe the chains:

Monosaccharides
: Single sugar units: glucose (the body's fuel), fructose (fruit sugar, handled mainly by the liver)
  and galactose (from milk).

Disaccharides
: Two units joined: sucrose, lactose and maltose. Most adults make less lactase, the enzyme that splits lactose, after childhood; this is the norm, and only some get symptoms (lactose intolerance; see the [*Digestion and absorption*](digestion-absorption.qmd) chapter).

Polysaccharides
: Long chains of units. Rice, bread and potato are mostly **starch**, a mix of amylose and
  amylopectin; **glycogen** is the animal store; and **cellulose**, dietary fibre, is held together by
  β-links that no human enzyme can cut, so it passes through.

Amylose and amylopectin
: The two forms of starch. Amylose is a straight chain with few ends and digests slowly; amylopectin
  is branched, with many ends, and digests fast. Glycogen is branched like amylopectin, but more
  highly.

![The same sugar unit, linked differently: one, two or many units, in straight (amylose), branched (amylopectin) or β-linked (cellulose) chains.](/figures/structures/carbohydrate-chains.svg){#fig-carb-chains fig-alt="Schematic of sugar units drawn as beads: one bead is a monosaccharide, two a disaccharide, many a polysaccharide; then a straight amylose chain, a branched amylopectin chain, and a beta-linked cellulose chain." width="520"}

Because the shape of the starch chain sets how fast it is digested, two kinds of the same grain can
differ:

::: {.example}
Glutinous ("sticky") rice is almost pure amylopectin and raises blood glucose sharply, while
high-amylose basmati sits lower. Even ordinary white rice raises blood glucose quickly (a high
glycaemic index, ~70+; see [Glycaemic index and glycaemic load](#sec-gi-gl)), so the amylose
advantage is real but relative [@atkinson2021gitables; @cai2021starchstructure].
:::

**What it does.** Carbohydrate is the body's main everyday fuel. Glucose powers the brain
(which normally depends on it almost exclusively) and fuels working muscle; the surplus is
stored as glycogen in liver and muscle, and adequate carbohydrate "spares" protein from
being burned for energy.

**From plate to cell.** Starch digestion begins in the mouth (salivary amylase) and resumes
in the small intestine (pancreatic amylase). There, brush-border enzymes (maltase, sucrase and
lactase, which sit on the surface of the intestinal lining cells) finish the breakdown to single
sugars. Glucose and galactose cross the gut lining on SGLT1 (sodium–glucose cotransporter 1), and
fructose on its own transporter, GLUT5. Glucose and galactose then travel to the liver in the
portal blood, where insulin drives their storage. (Digestion in detail: see the
[*Digestion and absorption*](digestion-absorption.qmd) chapter; the fed and fasted handling of glucose:
see the [*Integrative metabolism*](integrative-metabolism.qmd#sec-partB) chapter.)

**Quality: not all carbohydrate is equal.** In a major series of meta-analyses, higher fibre
and wholegrain intake was associated with roughly 15–30% lower all-cause and
cardiovascular mortality, and with lower rates of coronary disease, stroke, type 2 diabetes and
colorectal cancer. The association strengthened up to about 25–29 g of fibre a day
[@reynolds2019carb].

::: {.callout-warning}
## How strong is the fibre evidence?
The evidence comes mostly from prospective cohort studies (which record what people eat and follow
them forward for years), plus some trials. Its certainty is therefore moderate at best for fibre,
and lower for wholegrains and for glycaemic index and load (see
[Glycaemic index and glycaemic load](#sec-gi-gl)). These are associations, not proof of cause: the
benefit is real, but it carries that caveat.
:::

### Glycaemic index and glycaemic load {#sec-gi-gl}

Not all carbohydrate raises blood glucose at the same speed. **Available carbohydrate** is the
digestible carbohydrate in a food, the part that drives the glucose response. The **glycaemic
index (GI)** ranks a food by how much a portion containing 50 g of available carbohydrate raises
blood glucose over about two hours, relative to pure glucose, set at 100
[@atkinson2021gitables]. Lower-GI foods give a gentler, slower rise:

::: {.spectrum}
[Glycaemic index bands]{.tree-title}

- Low GI, 55 or less: most legumes, intact wholegrains, most whole fruit, milk
- Medium GI, 56–69: basmati rice, sweet potato
- High GI, 70 or more: white rice, white bread, glucose (100)

[Gentler rise]{.spectrum-end} [Faster, higher rise]{.spectrum-end}
:::

GI has a limitation: it fixes the carbohydrate at 50 g, which may be far from a real serving.
**Glycaemic load (GL)** corrects for this by scaling GI to the actual serving:

$$ \text{GL} = \frac{\text{GI} \times \text{available carbohydrate (g) per serving}}{100} $$

graded low ≤10, medium 11–19, high ≥20 per serving. GL therefore captures both the quality of
the carbohydrate (its GI) and the quantity actually eaten.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Should high-GI foods be avoided?
A high GI is often read as a reason to avoid a food, because a high GI means a bigger, faster
glucose rise.
Watermelon has a high GI (~76), yet a normal slice holds only ~6 g of carbohydrate, so its GL is
~5 (low): a small portion of a high-GI food can be a low-load choice. The reverse also holds: a
low-GI noodle such as *bee hoon* becomes a high-GL plate at hawker portions. Quality and portion
both matter, so GI alone is a poor guide to what to avoid.
:::

Explore the relationship below. Pick a food, and its GI sets the height of the glucose
curve; then drag the portion, which grows the shaded area (the glycaemic load). Switch
on *Compare* to see the watermelon-versus-potato paradox: near-identical peaks, very
different areas.

<div data-island="gi" data-src="/diagrams/glycemic-index-load.yml"></div>

Three caveats keep GI in proportion:

- GI is not a measure of healthiness: chocolate is low-GI.
- A food has no single fixed GI, because ripeness, processing, cooking and the rest of the meal all
  shift it.
- The evidence linking GI and GL to hard outcomes is the weakest strand of carbohydrate-quality
  research, of low to very low certainty, well below fibre and wholegrains [@reynolds2019carb].

For most patients the practical message is therefore the familiar one, not a GI number: favour
whole, intact, fibre-rich carbohydrates in sensible portions, the wholegrain quarter of My Healthy
Plate [@hpbHealthyPlate].

![Brown rice keeps its bran and germ: more fibre and a gentler glucose rise than white rice. Photo: Ceeseven, CC BY-SA 4.0.](/figures/food/brown-rice.jpg){#fig-brown-rice fig-alt="A bowl of cooked brown rice." width="320" .lightbox}

### From science to plate

::: {.callout-note}
## 🔬 Food science: what cooking does to starch
Cooking **gelatinises** starch: the granules swell and become easier to digest, so more thoroughly
cooked, finely milled starch raises glucose faster [@cai2021starchstructure]. When a cooked
starchy food is chilled, some starch **retrogrades** into **resistant starch**, which escapes
digestion and behaves partly like fibre. The effect is real but modest: a refinement of "quality
over quantity", not a way to make white rice "low-carb".
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## 🍜 Eating out
Four swaps improve the carbohydrate on a hawker plate [@hpbHealthyPlate; @hpbNutriGrade]:

- Choose the brown-rice or wholemeal option where offered.
- Ask for less rice and more vegetables.
- Order a *cai png* plate as "2 vegetables + 1 protein, less gravy".
- Pick a Nutri-Grade A or B drink, or plain water, over a Grade C or D one.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## 🍳 Healthy kitchen
Cook pasta and noodles *al dente*; cook, cool and, if wanted, reheat rice and potato to raise
resistant starch [@sonia2015rice]; and choose intact wholegrains (brown or red rice, rolled oats)
over products made from finely milled flour.
:::

### Fibre: the carbohydrate we don't digest {#sec-fibre}

**What it is.** Dietary fibre is carbohydrate that the small intestine cannot digest. It comes as
**soluble fibre** (viscous; in oats, legumes and some fruit) and **insoluble fibre** (bulking; in
wholegrain bran and vegetable skins), and much of it can be fermented by gut bacteria.

**What it does.** Soluble fibre slows digestion and blunts the rise in blood glucose; insoluble fibre adds
bulk and aids regularity; and the fermentable part feeds gut microbes that make short-chain fatty
acids (see [*The gut microbiome*](gut-microbiome.qmd#sec-scfa) chapter). Higher fibre intake is
among the best-supported dietary associations with lower disease risk (see the evidence above)
[@reynolds2019carb].

::: {.callout-note}
## 🔬 Food science: the food matrix, why whole fruit differs from juice
Fibre is part of a food's physical structure, its **food matrix**. Juicing or finely blending fruit
tears open the plant cell walls that enclosed the sugars. In a classic study, apple juice was drunk far
faster than the same carbohydrate as whole apples, satisfied less, and drew a larger insulin response
followed by a rebound fall in glucose [@haber1977apple]. A glass of juice also carries several fruits' worth of sugar with little of
the fibre. Intact cell walls slow sugar release; milling grain into fine flour destroys them, part of
the reason wholegrains are preferred to refined starch.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## 🍜 Eating out
Order whole fruit rather than bottled or freshly pressed juice, and add a vegetable or bean side, a
scoop of *dhal*, some *tau kwa*, chickpeas or extra *sayur*, to lift the fibre of an otherwise
refined-starch plate.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## 🍳 Healthy kitchen
Keep edible skins on (potato, apple, cucumber); eat fruit whole instead of juicing it; and stir
beans, lentils or rolled oats into everyday dishes for an easy fibre lift.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Check yourself: glutinous rice and basmati are both rice. Why does glutinous rice raise blood glucose more sharply?
Glutinous rice is almost pure amylopectin, a branched starch with many chain ends that digests fast.
Basmati carries more amylose, a straight chain with few ends that digests slowly, so its glucose rise
is gentler. The shape of the starch chain, as well as its size, sets the response, although ordinary
white rice is still high-GI.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Check yourself: watermelon has a higher GI than *bee hoon*. Why can a plate of *bee hoon* still be the bigger glucose load?
GI is measured on a fixed 50 g of available carbohydrate, so it rates the quality of the carbohydrate
but ignores how much is eaten. Glycaemic load scales GI to the real serving: a slice of watermelon
holds only about 6 g of carbohydrate (GL about 5, low), whereas a hawker portion of low-GI *bee hoon*
is a high-GL plate. Quality and portion both set the response.
:::

## Fat {#sec-dietary-fat}

**What it is.** Three variables generate every dietary fat: chain length, saturation and the
geometry of any double bonds. Five terms describe the molecules:

Fatty acid
: A hydrocarbon chain (a water-hating tail) capped by a carboxyl group, –COOH (a water-loving head).

Saturated fatty acid
: A fatty acid with no double bonds, so its straight chain packs tightly and the fat stays solid.

Unsaturated fatty acid
: A fatty acid with one double bond (monounsaturated) or more (polyunsaturated).

*Cis* and *trans*
: The two geometries of a double bond. A *cis* bond kinks the chain, giving liquid oils; a *trans*
  bond leaves it nearly straight, so *trans* fat behaves like a saturated one.

Essential fatty acids
: The two fatty acids the body cannot make: linoleic acid (an omega-6) and α-linolenic acid (an
  omega-3). The omega count runs from the tail end of the chain.

Fatty acids rarely travel alone. Three of them esterified onto a glycerol backbone make a
**triglyceride**, the main form of dietary and stored fat (and what the ~9 kcal/g refers to).
Chain length runs from short through medium to long; medium-chain fats are absorbed more directly,
which is the point of "MCT" (medium-chain triglyceride) oils. Replacing one fatty acid with a
phosphate head gives a **phospholipid**. Phospholipids are amphipathic (they have a water-loving
head and water-hating tails), so they self-assemble into the lipid bilayer of every cell membrane:
fat is a structural material as well as a fuel.

**Cholesterol** is a different, ring-shaped sterol that stabilises membranes and is the precursor of
steroid hormones, bile acids and vitamin D. The cholesterol in food raises blood cholesterol
less than saturated and *trans* fat do [@carson2020cholesterol].

![The major dietary lipids, as conventionally drawn. Three are fatty acids or built from them: a fatty acid is a hydrocarbon chain with a carboxyl head (the kink here is a *cis* double bond); three of them esterified onto a glycerol backbone make a triglyceride (the storage and dietary fat); and swapping one for a phosphate–choline head gives an amphipathic phospholipid (the main structural lipid of membranes). Cholesterol, by contrast, is a rigid four-ring sterol.](/figures/structures/lipid-classes.svg){#fig-lipid-classes fig-alt="Skeletal structures of four lipids, each labelled: cholesterol (four fused rings), a free fatty acid (a chain with a cis kink and a carboxyl group), a triglyceride (three fatty-acid chains on a glycerol backbone), and a phospholipid (two chains plus a phosphate–choline head)." width="430"}

Because fats do not dissolve in blood, they travel inside **lipoproteins**: chylomicrons,
very-low-density lipoprotein (VLDL), low-density lipoprotein (LDL) and high-density lipoprotein
(HDL). **LDL** delivers cholesterol and drives atherosclerosis (plaque formation in the artery wall)
when it builds up (lipoprotein handling: see the
[*Integrative metabolism*](integrative-metabolism.qmd#sec-lipoproteins) chapter).

**What it does.** Fat is the body's most concentrated energy store, a structural component of
every cell membrane, the carrier for the fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K), and the source of the
essential fatty acids.

**From plate to cell.** Fat does not mix with water, so it is emulsified first: bile salts from
the liver break it into tiny droplets, and pancreatic lipase frees fatty acids and
monoglycerides, which micelles carry to the gut lining for absorption. Inside the intestinal cells
these products are re-assembled into triglycerides and packaged into chylomicrons, which enter the
lymphatics (not the portal vein) before reaching the blood. (Bile and micelles: see the
[*Digestion and absorption*](digestion-absorption.qmd) chapter; lipoprotein transport and fat
metabolism: see the [*Integrative metabolism*](integrative-metabolism.qmd#sec-lipoproteins) chapter.)

**Quality: type matters more than total.** For decades the advice was "eat less fat"; the better
message is "eat better fat". Fats can be ranked by their relationship to cardiovascular risk:

::: {.spectrum}
[Dietary fats by cardiovascular risk]{.tree-title}

- *Trans* fat
- Saturated fat
- Monounsaturated fat
- Polyunsaturated fat, including omega-3

[Clearest harm]{.spectrum-end} [Most favourable]{.spectrum-end}
:::

The advice differs by type:

- *Trans* fat is the clearest harm. WHO recommends <1% of energy and elimination of industrial
  sources [@who2020diet].
- Saturated fat raises LDL cholesterol (the "bad" cholesterol); the practical advice is to replace
  it with unsaturated fat, rather than with refined carbohydrate.
- Mono- and polyunsaturated fats (olive oil, nuts, fish) are the ones to favour, and they include the
  essential omega-3 and omega-6 fatty acids.

![Nuts are a whole-food source of mono- and polyunsaturated fats. Photo: HaJunkiyada, CC BY-SA 4.0.](/figures/food/mixed-nuts.jpg){#fig-nuts fig-alt="An assortment of mixed nuts." width="320" .lightbox}

::: {.callout-note}
## Is a low-fat diet healthier?
Low-fat products look healthier because the long-standing advice was to eat less fat. Yet chasing
"low fat" often means swapping fat for refined starch or sugar, frequently a worse trade. The target
is fat quality, and the replacement nutrient matters. Where saturated fat sits within a whole food
(dairy versus processed meat) is still debated [@astrup2020satfat]; the message stays simple:
replace it with unsaturated fat and whole foods.
:::

### Fatty-acid geometry: *cis*, *trans* and saturated {#sec-cis-trans}

Oleic acid (olive oil) and elaidic acid (the classic industrial *trans* fat) contain the same atoms
and differ only in the geometry of one double bond. Start with the 2D formula, then rotate the 3D
model, and add stearic acid (a saturated fat) for comparison. The *trans* chain is almost as
straight as the saturated one, so, like stearic acid, it packs tightly and behaves like a solid fat.
The bend from one *cis* bond is modest; polyunsaturated fats, with several *cis* bonds, are far more
kinked.

<div data-island="molecule" data-src="/structures/dietary-fats.mol.yml"></div>

### From science to plate

::: {.callout-note}
## 🔬 Food science: geometry and oxidation
The *cis* kink in the model above is why olive oil is liquid while *trans* and saturated fats are
more solid. Heat matters too.
Overheating oil past its smoke point, or reusing frying oil repeatedly, oxidises and breaks it down into harmful compounds such as aldehydes; polyunsaturated oils are unstable under intense heat [@sfaReusingOils].
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## 🍜 Eating out
Four choices improve the fat in a hawker meal:

- Prefer steamed, grilled or stir-fried dishes over deep-fried ones.
- Ask for less oil.
- Skip the chicken skin.
- Choose fish as a protein where possible.

Some stalls reuse frying oil, which the Singapore Food Agency flags as a quality problem
[@sfaReusingOils].
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## 🍳 Healthy kitchen
Cook with unsaturated oils and don't heat them until they smoke; don't reuse frying oil again and
again; and reach for steaming, boiling or a light stir-fry over deep-frying. Fried foods draw in oil
and energy, and frequent intake tracks with higher type 2 diabetes and heart-failure risk
[@gadiraju2015fried].
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Check yourself: oleic acid and elaidic acid contain the same atoms. Why does elaidic acid behave like a saturated fat?
The two differ only in the geometry of one double bond. Oleic acid's *cis* bond kinks the chain, so
the molecules cannot pack tightly and olive oil stays liquid. Elaidic acid's *trans* bond leaves the
chain almost straight, like saturated stearic acid, so it packs tightly and behaves like a solid fat.
The shape of the chain, not its atoms, explains why *trans* fat behaves like saturated fat, in the
body as well as on the plate.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Check yourself: a patient cuts fat by switching to low-fat biscuits and more white bread. Why may his diet be no healthier?
Cutting fat often means replacing it with refined starch or sugar, which is frequently a worse trade.
The health effect depends on the type of fat and on what replaces it: saturated fat raises LDL
cholesterol, and the advice is to replace it with unsaturated fat, not with refined carbohydrate.
The goal is better fat, not less fat.
:::

## Protein {#sec-protein}

**What it is.** Protein is a polymer of **amino acids**. Every amino acid is built on one plan: a
central carbon carrying an amino group (–NH₂), a carboxyl group (–COOH), a hydrogen and a variable
side chain. Only the side chain differs between the ~20 amino acids. About nine are **essential
amino acids**: the body cannot make them, so they must come from the diet.

![L-alanine, a representative amino acid: an amino group (–NH₂), a carboxyl group (–COOH), and a variable side chain (here a methyl) that distinguishes one amino acid from another.](/figures/structures/l-alanine.svg){#fig-alanine fig-alt="Skeletal structure of the amino acid L-alanine." width="230"}

Amino acids link by **peptide bonds**, formed in a condensation reaction, into chains that fold at
four levels:

Primary structure
: The sequence of amino acids in the chain.

Secondary structure
: Local folding patterns: the α-helix and the β-sheet.

Tertiary structure
: The overall 3D fold of the chain.

Quaternary structure
: The assembly of several chains (subunits) into one molecule; haemoglobin has four.

Sequence sets shape, and shape sets function: a single amino-acid change in haemoglobin's sequence
causes sickle-cell disease.

The two real structures below show the last two levels: myoglobin is a single folded chain
(tertiary structure), and haemoglobin assembles four such chains (quaternary structure).

<div data-island="protein" data-src="/structures/proteins.protein.yml"></div>

**What it does.** Protein has structural and functional roles: it forms muscle, collagen and
skin, and it makes up enzymes, antibodies, and transport and signalling molecules. Individual amino
acids are also the precursors of other nitrogen-containing molecules, including several
neurotransmitters (such as serotonin and dopamine) and hormones (adrenaline, thyroid hormone).
Unlike carbohydrate and fat, protein is not primarily an energy store: the body keeps only a small
circulating amino-acid pool and turns its proteins over continuously.

**From plate to cell.** Protein digestion starts in the stomach, where acid unfolds it and
pepsin begins cleaving it. Pancreatic proteases (trypsin, chymotrypsin) and brush-border
peptidases then break it down to amino acids and short peptides, which are absorbed into the
portal blood.
Cells use these to build their own proteins; surplus amino acids are deaminated (the nitrogen
leaving as urea) and their carbon skeletons burned for energy or turned into glucose. (Digestion
in detail: see the [*Digestion and absorption*](digestion-absorption.qmd) chapter; amino-acid
metabolism: see the [*Integrative metabolism*](integrative-metabolism.qmd#sec-amino) chapter.)

**Quality: adequacy and completeness.** A useful population reference is about 0.8 g/kg/day,
adequate for most healthy adults [@who2007protein], though needs rise in older age, illness
[@bauer2013protage] and athletic training.
Protein also has the highest thermic effect of the macronutrients (see the
[*Energy balance*](energy-balance.qmd#sec-expenditure) chapter), contributing modestly to energy
expenditure and satiety.

**Protein quality** reflects how well a protein's amino acids match human needs and how digestible
it is. It is scored by the Protein Digestibility-Corrected Amino Acid Score (PDCAAS) and its
FAO-preferred successor, the Digestible Indispensable Amino Acid Score (DIAAS) [@fao2013protein].
Animal proteins are typically **complete** (not short of any essential amino acid). Most single
plant proteins are lower in one essential amino acid (cereals in lysine, legumes in methionine), so
**complementary** pairings such as rice and *dhal* cover each other's gaps across the day. Plant
protein foods also supply fibre and unsaturated fat.

![Tofu, a plant protein that also brings unsaturated fat, with no cholesterol. Photo: yearofeats, CC BY 2.0.](/figures/food/tofu.jpg){#fig-tofu fig-alt="Cubes of fresh tofu." width="320" .lightbox}

::: {.callout-note}
## 🔬 Food science: heat, browning and protein
Heat **denatures** protein, unfolding it so enzymes can reach it, which usually makes it easier to
digest: cooked egg protein is absorbed far better than raw (~91% vs ~51%) [@evenepoel1998egg]. But
the high-heat browning that adds flavour, the **Maillard reaction**, has a downside. In starchy
foods it forms **acrylamide**, a genotoxic carcinogen of concern [@efsa2015acrylamide]; in meat
cooked at high heat, related reactions of amino acids, sugars and creatine form heterocyclic amines,
and fat dripping onto a flame adds smoke-borne polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons; both are mutagens in
the laboratory, though the human cancer evidence is inconclusive [@nciCookedMeats].
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## 🍜 Eating out
Favour lean or plant proteins (fish, *tofu* or *tau kwa*, *dhal*, eggs, skinless chicken) over fatty
or processed meats, and go easy on heavily charred satay or barbecue.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## 🍳 Healthy kitchen
Aim for golden, not brown, when frying or roasting, and don't blacken food [@fsaGoForGold]; gentle
methods (poaching, steaming, braising) cook protein well without the high-heat by-products.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Check yourself: why can a single amino-acid change in haemoglobin cause sickle-cell disease?
The amino-acid sequence (the primary structure) determines how the chain folds (secondary and
tertiary structure) and how chains assemble (quaternary structure), and that shape determines what
the protein does. Changing one
amino acid in haemoglobin's sequence can therefore change the protein's shape, and with it its
function, enough to cause disease: sequence sets shape, and shape sets function.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Check yourself: rice and *dhal* are each low in one essential amino acid. Why does eating them across the day still supply every essential amino acid?
Cereals such as rice are low in lysine and legumes such as *dhal* are low in methionine, so each
supplies what the other lacks. Because the body cannot make essential amino acids, what matters is
that the day's mix supplies all of them: complementary plant proteins cover each other's gaps.
:::

## From nutrients to patterns {#sec-nutrient-patterns}

Modern guidelines have moved decisively from "hit this macronutrient ratio" to "eat these foods,
in this pattern" [@aha2021diet]. There is no single ideal macronutrient split: guidelines
deliberately avoid prescribing one. Diabetes standards, for example, find no ideal percentage of
energy from carbohydrate, protein or fat, and advise individualising the split and referring to a
dietitian [@ada2026standards]. Their consistent themes are to favour wholegrains, plants and
unsaturated fats, and to minimise added sugar, *trans* fat, sodium and ultra-processed foods.
(Dietary patterns in full: see the [*What a healthy diet looks like*](dietary-guidelines-patterns.qmd)
chapter.)

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Check yourself: two diets share the same split of 50% carbohydrate, 30% fat and 20% protein. Why might one be far healthier?
A macronutrient split says nothing about form or food source: the carbohydrate could come from
wholegrains and vegetables or from white rice and sugary drinks, and the fat from nuts and fish or
from fried food. This is why guidelines advise eating patterns (wholegrains, plants and unsaturated
fats; little added sugar, *trans* fat, sodium and ultra-processed food) instead of one ideal ratio.
:::

## Are carbs bad? {#sec-close}

The question has no single answer until it becomes *which carbohydrate, from what food?* A sugary
drink with a plate of white rice, and a bowl of brown rice with vegetables and fish, are both
"carbs", and they are not remotely the same for health. In clinic, the task is to give quality
guidance ("more wholegrains, fewer free sugars, better fat"), base it on My Healthy Plate, and
refer to a dietitian when a patient wants a restrictive or therapeutic diet [@ada2026standards].
Prescribing grams is not the task at this stage.

## The Singapore picture {#sec-singapore}

My Healthy Plate ("quarter, quarter, half": ¼ wholegrains, ¼ protein, ½ fruit and vegetables)
[@hpbHealthyPlate] and the Nutri-Grade A–D drink labels [@hpbNutriGrade] are Singapore's everyday
tools for the advice above (both introduced in the
[*Why nutrition matters*](01-why-nutrition-matters.qmd) chapter). The National Nutrition Survey
2022 shows the gap they address: only about 4% of the staples eaten are wholegrain, against a
recommendation of about 30%; saturated fat makes up a large share of fat intake; and most residents
exceed the sodium target [@mohNNS2022]. The gap between what the science recommends and what the
population actually eats is where a brown-rice swap, a less oily order and a plainer drink make a
difference.
